documentation.title: Large sliding: the gap follows the surface the body slides onto
documentation.description:
Gate for the kinematics of slidingType="large", and the first testcase in the suite that can tell "large" from "small" at all.
Every other contact testcase has a FLAT interface, so a body can slide along it without the gap responding and small-sliding kinematics happen to be exact. Here the primary surface is a shallow tent built from two straight LINE3 faces meeting at an apex, so tangential motion moves a secondary point to a different height, and a point crossing the apex has to re-pair onto the other primary element with a different normal.
The upper body's flat interface is given a rigid tangential displacement of 0.7 in x. Geometry only: applyContactForce="no", so nothing depends on an elasticity solution and every number is arithmetic on the mesh.
With integrationOrder="2" the secondary element carries two Gauss points. Both end up on the RIGHT face; the first started on the left face and therefore crossed the apex. Small-sliding kinematics predict something different and computable: they freeze the pairing and the normal at u = 0 and evaluate g = g_0 + (u_s - u_m).n with the ORIGINAL normal. The two formulations differ by 28 % on minGap, and the reference records the large-sliding value; switching this testcase to slidingType="small" reproduces the other one, which is how it gates the feature rather than merely exercising it.
numContactElements is the second, discrete half of the assertion. There is one assembler element per (secondary, primary) pair, so the count is 2 initially -- the two Gauss points sit on opposite faces -- and must fall to 1 once both have slid onto the right face. Under small sliding it stays 2, because the pairing is frozen by definition. A continuous quantity can drift; this one cannot.
Note what small sliding gets RIGHT: the point that stayed on its own face. A flat face is exactly where the frozen-normal assumption holds, which is why a testcase built on flat interfaces can never expose the difference.
segmentation="gpts" is deliberate: it puts the integration points at the secondary element's own 2-point Gauss rule, so the expected values are a two-line hand calculation rather than the outcome of a cut.
